bollymeter.basis: An 8.0 IMDb rating from a substantial international viewer base and a MyDramaList score of 8.7 across 13,558 users place this firmly in the upper tier of Korean crime procedurals. Kim Nam-gil's Daesang win at the SBS Drama Awards anchors a critical consensus that the lead performance alone elevates the material.

pull_quotes.text: Through the Darkness breaks away from the conventional format and sheds light on those who look into the cases.

seasons.review_body: Through the Darkness aired on SBS from January to March 2022, adapted from the memoir of Kwon Il-yong, Korea's first criminal profiler. The series follows Song Ha-young as he and his team at the Criminal Behaviour Analysis Unit reconstruct the psychology of serial killers from the 1980s and 90s, a period when Korean law enforcement had no vocabulary for behavioural evidence. Kim Nam-gil won the SBS Daesang for his performance - reserved, methodical, and haunted - which reviewers consistently identified as the anchor of the entire series. The procedural structure is deliberately unglamorous: investigations unfold through paperwork, interviews, and incremental insight rather than thriller set-pieces. The MyDramaList community scored it 8.7 out of 10 across more than 13,500 ratings, placing it among the best-reviewed crime dramas of 2022 on that platform. Critics who covered the show praised its patient storytelling and the authenticity it draws from the source material.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.review_body:
# Through The Darkness S1E1: "Episode 1" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

A child loses a balloon in the opening chaos, and the hour lets that small accident sit beside a body found in cold water. The cut is blunt. One moment has movement, noise, panic over something harmless. The next has the shape of a case, the kind that will harden into news copy, suspicion, and bad police certainty. An unknown voice says, "That's how they found her." That line becomes the episode's method. The premiere cares less about the shock of death than the dangerous story built around it. BollyAI's read: the premiere works because it treats a wrong answer as its first villain.

## The Case Begins With a Story Already Half-Written

The premiere opens like a procedural that does not trust procedure yet. The Red Cap Incident is already being filtered through news reports, break-ins at multiplex houses, and public language that turns fear into shorthand. By the time the closing news describes the break-ins linked to Red Cap, the episode has made its first clean point: a name can arrive before the truth does.

That matters because the hour keeps showing how quickly a case becomes a shape everyone wants to fill. A culprit known as Red Cap is attached to **Choi Hwa Yeon**, and the story moves toward a woman in her twenties found dead, "with all of her clothes undressed." The detail is ugly, but the writing uses it as procedural pressure rather than shock decoration. It changes the kind of crime being discussed. It changes what the police think they are chasing. It changes how suspicion can be sold.

The hour refuses to give the investigation a clean emotional runway. It introduces noise first: news, assumptions, case labels, fragments of motive, the public shape of a criminal act. That gives the episode its spine. This is a story about how evidence gets crowded by narrative.

The weakness is visible early. The dossier points to bursts of dialogue around the investigative beats, and the premiere can feel loaded with setup language. Some of that is useful. Some of it presses too hard. Still, the core is sharp: the police are hunting a killer while fighting the convenience of a conclusion.

## Song Ha Young Hears the Wrong Note

**Song Ha Young** enters the hour through resistance. He wants to help solve the case, but more importantly, he does not want the real culprit to slip away under a pile of official confidence. He is surrounded by a system ready to link **Bang Ki Hoon** to Choi Hwa Yeon's murder, yet he questions that assumption even after the case begins to look settled.

That makes him legible without a grand speech. His job is not to be the loudest detective in the room. His job is to hear the wrong note in the arrangement. When a supervisor orders the team to investigate Bang Ki Hoon in connection with the Red Cap case, the episode pushes Ha Young into the place where he works best: between command and doubt.

The arrest beat gives the police a neat line of action. Bang Ki Hoon is brought in on suspicion of Choi Hwa Yeon's murder. The case suddenly has a name, a relationship, a direction. A line like "She's my girlfriend" links him directly to the victim and gives the arrest its practical logic. The episode understands why that logic is tempting. It also makes Ha Young's unease feel necessary rather than contrarian.

BollyAI's read: Ha Young is interesting here because his doubt is not theatrical. He is no genius posing above fools. The hour frames him as a man who understands that a forced ending can be more dangerous than an unsolved beginning. That is the premiere's best character move. It gives the lead a moral engine before it gives him a mythology.

## A Confession Is Not Closure

The hour's boldest procedural idea is that confession does not end the case. It can become another trap. The dossier's central contradiction notes Ha Young questioning the assumption around Bang Ki Hoon even after a confession, arguing that the case may be over or forced. That is the episode's thesis in its cleanest form.

The arrest gives the story momentum, but the later announcement that "He's not the culprit" detonates the comfort of that momentum. The beat plays less like cheap surprise and more like the episode correcting its own apparent direction. The police had a suspect. The case had pressure. The audience had a track to follow. Then the track breaks.

This is where the writing feels most purposeful. The episode does not ask whether Bang Ki Hoon is suspicious in some abstract way. It asks whether suspicion has been allowed to replace proof. That question fits the hour's larger pattern: Red Cap as label, Choi Hwa Yeon as public name, the murder as a fresh wound, and Ha Young as the one person trying to keep the investigation from mistaking shape for substance.

The craft is rougher when the show has to explain its procedural thinking. The tone notes suggest mid-episode silences and shifts into explanation or testing rather than constant banter, and that can make parts of the hour feel more instructional than dramatic. But the gear change has value. It slows the case down long enough for doubt to gather weight.

The result is a premiere that earns its best reversal. When the episode says Bang Ki Hoon is not the culprit, it clears a suspect and condemns the route that made him convenient.

## The Pattern Is Smarter Than the Police Want It to Be

The open loops are where the premiere starts to look larger than a single murder. Patterned wall numbers appear across multiple women’s and kids’ homes. Planned-crime behavior enters the frame, including the erasing of footprints and fingerprints. These details matter because they point away from impulse and toward design.

That changes the threat. A crime of rage can still be brutal, but a planned crime has a colder grammar. It leaves marks by choosing what not to leave. It builds absence into evidence. The episode uses those possibilities to make the real culprit feel present without revealing too much. The unknown has method.

Here, the premiere finds a cleaner rhythm than in its heavier explanatory patches. The pattern work gives the investigation a texture beyond interrogation and arrest. Wall numbers, cleaned traces, break-ins, and the Red Cap label sit in the same uneasy field. The hour invites the viewer to ask what connects them, but it does not flatten the mystery into a puzzle box. The human cost stays nearby because the body in cold water and the description of the victim's condition keep dragging the case back from abstraction.

The episode does plant many investigative hooks at once. Red Cap, Bang Ki Hoon, Choi Hwa Yeon, the wall numbers, planned erasure of evidence, and the question of false attribution all compete for space. The hour survives because the central line is strong. Without Ha Young's suspicion holding it together, the premiere could have felt like a case board introduced too quickly.

## The Verdict

"Episode 1" is a sturdy, tense premiere that understands how frightening certainty can be when it arrives too early. Its best material comes from Song Ha Young refusing the comfort of a solved case and from the episode's insistence that labels, confessions, and public narratives can distort the hunt for truth. The pacing is uneven when the hour leans into procedural explanation, and a few planted mysteries crowd the frame. Still, the case construction carries the weight. BollyAI's score: 7.8. As a season opener, it sets Ha Young against the killer and against every shortcut that helps the killer stay hidden.

Written by BollyAI, reviewed by our editorial team.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere establishes the procedural in its most stripped-down form - a detective who believes in reading crime scenes the way a psychologist reads a patient, at a time when Korean law enforcement considers that approach frivolous. The period detail and Kim Nam-gil's physical restraint make an immediate case for the show's seriousness.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Song Ha-young's first walk through a crime scene - the camera following his gaze as he reconstructs motive from evidence most officers are already bagging for court.

verdict.one_liner: A sharp procedural opener where Song Ha Young’s doubt turns a convenient arrest into the episode’s real crime scene.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 12
episode_reviews.review_body: Through the Darkness Season 1 Episode 12 aired March 12, 2022 on SBS as the season finale. IMDb audiences scored the series 8.0; MyDramaList rated it 8.7 from over 13,500 users; Kim Nam-gil won the SBS Daesang. ZAPZEE noted the series 'sheds light on those who look into the cases' - and the finale is where that focus pays off completely. The episode delivers the personal toll that twelve episodes of unglamorous procedural work has been accumulating: the cost of looking at serial killer psychology for a decade, the cost of being right when institutions do not want to believe you, and the cost of the specific institutional validation the unit finally receives. The resolution is quiet in the same register as the method it embodies - no dramatic catharsis, no score-driven release, simply the formal acknowledgment that the work was real and that it mattered. The Daesang recognises a performance that sustains that register across twelve episodes without relief.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale delivers the personal cost accumulated across twelve episodes and closes on the unit's institutional legitimation - earned, not given. The emotional resolution is as quiet as the procedural method it embodies.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The team's formal recognition by a sceptical institution - the scene that confirms the unit's survival and the human price paid for it.
